tier_reason: The only numbers are one informal third-party run in the pRDS README (i7 Mac, no CPU model, no tool versions, no repeats, author calls it 'not in an entirely scientific manner'); pRDS is not a well-known benchmark suite and pixz's own repo has no benchmark, so this is numbers without methodology, tier C.

corrections.baseline: xz (XZ Utils), run multi-threaded by pRDS with the same core count as pixz (xz -zcT<cores> -6 to compress, xz -cdT<cores> to decompress)
corrections.workload: Write and read an R object holding a 3 GB CSV of about 17 million tweets through the R package pRDS, which pipes R's serialization stream into external compressors at default levels: pixz -tp<cores> -6 versus xz -zcT<cores> -6 for writing, pixz -dp<cores> versus xz -cdT<cores> for reading (cores = mc.cores option, or detectCores()/2 when unset), on a 4-core, 8-thread i7 Mac. Benchmark committed 2020-06-02.
corrections.claimed_speedup: pRDS README benchmark table: pixz write 443 s, read 63 s, size 805 MB versus multi-threaded xz write 469 s, read 64 s, size 795 MB (pixz about 1.06x faster to compress and about 1.02x faster to decompress, output about 1.3% larger, derived from page data). Other xz-format rows: 7z (-mmt) 580 s write, 83 s read, 741 MB; R native xzfile 2626 s write, 105 s read, 772 MB (pixz about 5.9x faster than R's built-in single-threaded xz, but multi-threaded xz itself is about 5.6x faster than R native, derived from page data, so that gap is threading, not pixz). R native uncompressed write and read take 99 s and 42 s, which bounds the read rows.
corrections.caveats: Weak evidence: one loosely controlled run by a third party in an obscure R package (pRDS, GPL-2.0, 0 stars; the pRDS author says 'not in an entirely scientific manner', 'loosely controlled environment', and that four tools did not work as intended on the machine), no tool versions, no flags, no CPU model, no repeat runs. pRDS's command table (R/zzz.R) runs xz as 'xz -zcT# -%' and 'xz -cdT#' and pixz as 'pixz -tp# -%' and 'pixz -dp#' with the same core count, so the xz row is multi-threaded xz, not single-threaded: the result is pixz versus xz -T at equal threads, a 6% compression gap that a single run cannot separate from noise. Reads go through R's deserializer from a pipe (uncompressed read alone takes 42 s), so the 63 s versus 64 s read rows are R-bound and say little about pixz's parallel decompression; the benchmark predates xz 5.4's multi-threaded decompression. The pixz README makes no speed numbers; its claims are that it parallelizes decompression, indexes tarballs for random access, and defaults to all cores while xz defaults to one (modern xz has -T and -T0, so that is a default difference). No stronger public pixz-versus-xz measurement was found (two WebSearch queries returned only README mirrors). Not clearly faster than multi-threaded xz; its distinct value is the block index for random access to tarball members.

notes: Numbers match the pRDS README exactly and metadata checks out (BSD-2-Clause, 795 stars, 66 forks, not archived, last commit 2025-03-08, stale). The record's caveat that the xz row might be single-threaded was wrong: pRDS passes -T<cores> to xz, so record the shortcoming as 'about 6% faster than multi-threaded xz in one informal third-party run; not clearly faster; read rows bound by R deserialization'. Judged against general-lossless's xz baseline.

tier_reason: Public benchmark code (src/BenchMuParser2.cpp, src/BenchTinyExpr.cpp, src/ParserBench.cpp in ArashPartow/math-parser-benchmark-project), compiler MSVC 1913 with Release flags in math-parser-benchmark-project/math-parser-benchmark-project_msvc2017.vcxproj, and CPU model Intel Xeon E5-2687W in the logs; the suite is third-party to muparser, so A (consistent with the ExprTk entry from the same suite).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README per-expression example '(a^2/sin(2*pi/b))-a/2': muparser 2.2.4 47.358 ns, TinyExpr 121.184 ns, Lepton 297.673 ns, muparserx 498.809 ns (muparser about 2.6x faster than TinyExpr, derived from page data); but in the README's second example '+a^+b+1.1' TinyExpr 53.620 ns beats muparser 66.387 ns. README example summary (bench_expr.txt): muparser 2.2.4 517 points (score 37), TinyExpr 354 (31), MTParser 381 (34), MathExpr 360 (29), Lepton 134 (8), muparserx 86 (5), versus FParser 4.5 584 (43), atmsp 530 (38), METL 686 (52) and ExprTk 901 (100). Committed 2018 log (logs/shootout_20180421_00.zip, Shootout_20180420_182359.txt, bench_expr.txt): muparser 523 points (score 38), TinyExpr 360 (32), MTParser 383 (34), MathExpr 364 (30), Lepton 136 (8), muparserx 85 (5). Score is the mean of per-expression (ExprTk time / parser time) x 100, so muparser averages about 1.2x TinyExpr's per-expression speed on bench_expr.txt (38/32, derived from page data); on the larger 2018 suites the gap is wider: bench_expr_complete.txt 28 versus 15 (about 1.9x), bench_expr_extensive.txt 24 versus 12 (about 2.0x), bench_expr_random_without_functions.txt 28 versus 13 (about 2.2x), but on bench_expr_weird.txt TinyExpr wins (508 points, score 46, versus muparser 394, score 35).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: MSVC Version 1913 (Visual Studio 2017, toolset v141), Release|Win32 (32-bit) per math-parser-benchmark-project/math-parser-benchmark-project_msvc2017.vcxproj: Optimization MaxSpeed (/O2), InlineFunctionExpansion AnySuitable, IntrinsicFunctions, FavorSizeOrSpeed Speed, WholeProgramOptimization, FloatingPointModel Precise, NDEBUG, _SECURE_SCL=0 (flags read from the current HEAD project file; the result logs print only compiler version and build type). The repo's math-parser-benchmark-project.pro builds with g++ -std=c++11 -march=native -fopenmp and -O3, with HAVE_STDINT_H and MUP_USE_OPENMP defined.
corrections.caveats: Mixed result: muparser 2.2.4 is 7th of 13 entries by points on bench_expr.txt (behind ExprTk, ExprTkFloat, muparserSSE, METL, FParser and atmsp) and loses to ExprTk, METL and FParser on every 2018 suite, so 'faster' holds only against TinyExpr, MTParser, MathExpr, Lepton and its heavier sibling muParserX; even TinyExpr beats it on bench_expr_weird.txt and on some single expressions. The suite is maintained by ExprTk's author, a competitor, and bundles muparser 2.2.4 (the README says the archive 'may contain outdated versions'); current muparser is 2.3.6 (released 2026-04-10) with many later bug fixes, so the 2018 numbers may not apply to it. The 'omp' variant is slower than plain muparser in every log read. Logged results are Windows 32-bit MSVC only, from 2018; the README summary is labelled an example. The harness pre-evaluates once to build bytecode outside the timed loop and swaps variables each iteration, and disqualifies wrong results per expression (muparser had 0 failures). The project's own site (beltoforion.de) was not read. Licence note: the benchmark README lists muParser as MIT; the repo LICENSE read today is BSD-2-Clause.

notes: Numbers match the suite README and the committed 2018 log; corrected the rank (7th, not 6th, by points) and added that TinyExpr wins on bench_expr_weird.txt and on the README's '+a^+b+1.1' example, so the 2.6x headline is one favourable expression and the suite-average gain over TinyExpr is about 1.2x to 2.2x depending on the file. Metadata checks out (BSD-2-Clause, 532 stars, 142 forks, last commit 2026-07-03, active, release 2.3.6). Shortcoming to record: mid-pack in its own shootout, slower than ExprTk, METL, FParser and atmsp; numbers are on muparser 2.2.4 from 2018, 32-bit MSVC.

tier_reason: First-party README tables with the CPU named only as Sapphire Rapids, no flags or run counts and no named benchmark code for the library tables, so tier C, the same tier as the existing entry.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Dot product (single 2048-d, single-threaded, Sapphire Rapids): f32 7.1 gso/s versus NumPy+OpenBLAS 1.5 (about 4.7x, derived from page data), PyTorch+MKL 0.6, JAX 0.4; f64 5.8 versus 2.0, 0.6, 0.4; bf16 9.7 versus 0.5 (PyTorch, JAX); f16 11.5 versus 0.2 (NumPy), 0.5 (PyTorch), 0.4 (JAX); i8 14.8 versus 1.1 (NumPy, overflowing). Matmul 2048x2048 single-threaded: i8 1279 gso/s versus PyTorch+MKL 50.0; e5m2 398 versus 0.4 (PyTorch) and about 26.4 (JAX); but slower than the BLAS-backed rows for f64 8.6 versus 65.5 (NumPy+OpenBLAS) and 68.2 (PyTorch+MKL), f32 37.7 versus 140 and 145, bf16 458 versus 851 (PyTorch), and f16 103 versus 140 (PyTorch). GCC 12 table: f16 inner product 5,990 K/s versus GCC f16 192 K/s (31x) and GCC f32 3,810 K/s (about 1.6x, derived from page data); Jensen-Shannon f16 2,140 K/s versus GCC f16 18 K/s (118x) and GCC f32 1,180 K/s (about 1.8x, derived from page data). Binary size: 5 MB versus NumPy+OpenBLAS 30 MB, JAX 357 MB, PyTorch+MKL 705 MB.

notes: Known project under another URL: this is the already-verified wave 1 entry 'NumKong (formerly SimSIMD)', id https://github.com/ashvardanian/simsimd (github.com/ashvardanian/SimSIMD serves the NumKong repository), so record decision duplicate. The README numbers in this record are accurate and add what the existing entry lacks (NumPy/PyTorch/JAX dot-product and matmul tables, including the f64, f32, bf16 and f16 matmul rows where NumKong is slower than OpenBLAS or MKL); fold them into the SimSIMD entry's claim and caveats via a retier file. Metadata here checks out: Apache-2.0, 1.9k stars, last commit 2026-10-05, active.
